title: Resolution of the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture

concept.text: A proof or disproof that the rank of the group of rational points of an elliptic curve over the rationals equals the order of vanishing of its L-function at s = 1. Sources given: https://www.claymath.org/millennium-problems/ ; https://world-of-mathematics.com/blog/millennium-problems-overview/.

page.title: Resolution of the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer rank conjecture
page.definition: A proof or counterexample settles rank E(ℚ) = ordₛ₌₁ L(E,s) for every elliptic curve over ℚ, a nonsingular projective cubic with a rational point. Rank counts independent infinite-order generators of rational points; the right side is the vanishing order at s = 1 of the L-function built from counts of points modulo primes.

goal.need: A proof would tell us when an elliptic curve over ℚ has infinitely many rational points: exactly when L(E,1)=0. For an odd square-free integer n>0, count the integer triples satisfying 2x²+y²+8z²=n and those satisfying 2x²+y²+32z²=n. If the first count differs from twice the second, no right triangle with rational sides has area n. A proof would make equality sufficient as well. Together with the corresponding test for even n, this would certify the computed list of such areas through 10¹².

statements.body: Clay Mathematics Institute, Board of Directors
statements.quote: with $1 million allocated to the solution of each problem.
statements.context: The allocation applies to each Millennium Prize Problem.

The introduction to The Millennium Prize Problems lists the conjecture among the seven problems selected by the founding Scientific Advisory Board and announced at the Collège de France on 24 May 2000.

completion.title: A complete resolution of the rank conjecture meets Clay’s Millennium Prize acceptance criteria.
completion.criterion: Prove rank E(ℚ) = ordₛ₌₁ L(E,s) for every elliptic curve E/ℚ, or provide a counterexample that Clay judges effectively resolves the problem. The solution must be published in a Qualifying Outlet under §6 of Clay’s rules; at least two years must pass after publication; and Clay must determine that it has general acceptance in the global mathematics community and satisfactorily answers the official problem.
completion.set_by: Clay Mathematics Institute, official problem description and Millennium Prize Description and Rules, §§4–7.
completion.threshold_quote: the Proposed Solution has satisfactorily answered the questions raised by the Problem’s official description, as determined in the sole discretion of CMI.
completion.basis: Clay’s official description specifies rank equality and identifies the leading-coefficient formula separately as a refinement. Its rules establish the acceptance procedure.

milestones.title: Elliptic curves over ℚ with complex multiplication and L(E,1)≠0 have rank zero.
milestones.criterion: For every elliptic curve E/ℚ with complex multiplication, prove that L(E,1)≠0 implies rank E(ℚ)=0. Here complex multiplication means that over an algebraic closure the curve admits endomorphisms other than multiplication by integers.
milestones.set_by: Clay’s official problem description, §2, gives the general formulation over ℚ. Theorem 1 of Coates and Wiles states the result for complex multiplication by the ring of integers of an imaginary quadratic field of class number 1.
milestones.threshold_quote: with complex multiplication and L(C, 1) ≠ 0, then C(Q) is finite.

milestones.title: Every elliptic curve over ℚ with analytic rank 0 or 1 satisfies rank equality.
milestones.criterion: For every elliptic curve E/ℚ, prove both implications. If L(E,1)≠0, then rank E(ℚ)=0. If L(E,1)=0 and L′(E,1)≠0, then rank E(ℚ)=1.
milestones.set_by: Mathematical community: Gross–Zagier–Kolyvagin theorem and modularity; stated in Clay’s official description, §2.
milestones.threshold_quote: m = 0 or 1, then the conjecture holds.

milestones.title: At least 66.48% of elliptic curves over ℚ, ordered by height, satisfy rank equality.
milestones.criterion: Among elliptic curves E/ℚ of height H(E)<X, prove that the proportion satisfying rank E(ℚ)=ordₛ₌₁ L(E,s) has limit inferior at least 0.6648 as X→∞. Count each ℚ-isomorphism class once using its nonsingular model y²=x³+Ax+B with A,B∈ℤ and no prime p for which both p⁴ divides A and p⁶ divides B. Set H(E)=max(4|A|³,27B²).
milestones.set_by: Mathematical community: Bhargava–Skinner–Zhang, Theorem 1 and equation (1).

milestones.title: Rank equality holds unconditionally for 100% of elliptic curves over ℚ ordered by height.
milestones.criterion: Among ℚ-isomorphism classes with H(E)<X, using the integral models and height in m3, prove unconditionally that the proportion satisfying rank E(ℚ)=ordₛ₌₁ L(E,s) tends to 1 as X→∞. An exceptional set of density zero is allowed.
milestones.set_by: Mathematical community: density-one conclusion explicitly formulated in Bhargava–Skinner–Zhang, Theorem 27; proved there only conditionally.
milestones.threshold_quote: the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer rank conjecture is true for 100% of elliptic curves over Q.

milestones.title: Finite products of point counts distinguish elliptic curves of different rational ranks in examples.
milestones.criterion: For elliptic curves E/ℚ of independently determined ranks, compute Nₚ, the number of projective points modulo p, and tabulate ∏ₚ≤ₓ(Nₚ/p) as x increases. Exhibit the observed association between the growth of the product and the rank across the examples.
milestones.set_by: B. J. Birch and H. P. F. Swinnerton-Dyer, Notes on elliptic curves. II, §1, experiment of autumn 1958.
milestones.threshold_quote: the rate of increase of f(P) was fairly closely correlated with the number of generators of infinite order

milestones.title: Rank equality is verified for every elliptic curve over ℚ of conductor at most 5077.
milestones.criterion: For every ℚ-isogeny class of elliptic curves of conductor N≤5077, establish that the rank of the rational points equals the order of vanishing of L(E,s) at s=1. It suffices to check one representative per class because both ranks are invariant under isogeny.
milestones.set_by: J. E. Cremona, Algorithms for Modular Elliptic Curves, second edition, chapter IV, summary of computations through conductor 5077.
milestones.threshold_quote: we have to date carried out the computations described above for all levels N up to 5077.

not_found: No externally prescribed milestone sequence or uniquely defined penultimate theorem was found in Clay’s documents or the rank-density literature.
No statement questioning the value or feasibility of resolving the rank conjecture was found in the prize documents or mathematical society publications searched.

results.finding: All modular elliptic curves over ℚ of analytic rank at most 1 satisfy rank equality.
results.quote: Theorem 1. The equality r(E) = ar(E) holds and ill(E) is finite if ar(E) ~ 1 .

results.finding: For elliptic curves over ℚ satisfying Theorem 9’s hypotheses, both ranks equal 1.
results.detail: The rank-zero theorem allows odd primes p. The rank-one theorem requires p ≥ 5. Both are theorems about families without a finite sample size.
results.quote: Then the rank and analytic rank of E are both equal to 1.

results.finding: Among all elliptic curves over ℚ below a growing height cutoff, at least 66.48% satisfy rank equality.
results.quote:
Corollary 26 When ordered by height, at least 66.48% of elliptic curves over Q have algebraic and
analytic rank 0 or 1.

results.finding: Among all elliptic curves over ℚ ordered by height, 100% satisfy rank equality under the Selmer-average hypothesis.
results.detail: The source reports the required Selmer averages for p = 2, 3, and 5. Theorem 27 assumes the formula for all primes.
results.quote:
Suppose that for
all primes p, the average size of the p-Selmer group of elliptic curves over Q is p + 1. Then the
Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer rank conjecture is true for 100% of elliptic curves over Q.

results.finding: Every modular elliptic curve over ℚ whose L-function has a simple zero at s = 1 has rational rank at least 1.
results.detail: Theorem (7.3) relates the first derivative to the canonical height of a rational point. A nonzero height gives an infinite-order point and hence the lower bound.
results.quote:
we will show that any modular elliptic curve over Q whose L-function has a 
simple zero at s= 1 contains rational points of infinite order.

results.finding: Across four elliptic curves, higher algebraic rank tracks faster growth of the partial product through X = 100,000.
results.quote: Here the slope against log log X grows with the rank of each curve.

results.finding: Every CM elliptic curve E/ℚ with L(E,1) ≠ 0 has Mordell–Weil rank 0.
results.quote:
Any CM elliptic curve E/Q with L(E/Q, 1) ⁄= 0 satisﬁes the assumptions
of Corollary 2.

results.finding: All elliptic curves over ℚ of analytic rank at most 1 have Mordell–Weil rank equal to their analytic rank.
results.detail: Theorem 4.4 proves the equality using the Gross–Zagier–Zhang formula and Kolyvagin’s theorem. The conductor bound applies to the separate computation of the full BSD formula.
results.quote: It follows that the rank of E(Q) is equal to ran(E/Q).

results.finding: Mordell–Weil and analytic ranks agree for all 568,824 ℚ-isogeny classes tabulated below conductor 130,000.
results.detail: The source gives a class count for the broader range. It identifies the work as part of a volume but does not establish journal peer review, independent replication of the rank checks, or proof-assistant verification.
results.quote:
In all cases
where the analytic rank is 2 or 3 we have veriﬁed by 2-descent that the rank is
equal to the analytic rank. When the analytic rank is 0 or 1 this is known to be
true by results of Rubin, Kolyvagin and Gross and Zagier.

results.finding: For one ℚ-isogeny class of conductor 5077, the rational rank and the L-series vanishing order at s = 1 both equal 3.
results.detail: The authors use a Heegner-point height bound to deduce exact vanishing of L′(1) and compute a nonzero cubic coefficient with a tail estimate.
results.quote:
The elliptic curve y2 = 4x3 - 28x + 25 has rank 3 over Q. Assuming the Weil- 
Taniyama conjecture for this curve, we show that its L-series L(s) has a triple zero at s = 1
